mainTopic: Laws of individual and communal fasts: shoes, postponing a fast, dream fasts, and the escalating fasts for rain
overview: This amud first finishes defining 'dozing,' a state that is half-asleep and half-awake. It then teaches in the name of רב that an individual who accepts a fast may not wear shoes, out of concern that he meant a communal fast. To avoid this, he can say clearly that it is a תענית יחיד. The גמרא then describes how different sages handled shoes on fast days, and notes that in בבל the only full communal fast is תשעה באב. Next, רב rules that a person may 'borrow' his private fast and repay it later. שמואל's reaction is reported in two opposite versions. A story then shows that a תענית חלום cannot be postponed: it works only on that same day, even on שבת, and fasting on שבת requires a make-up fast. A new משנה lays out the stages of fasting for rain: three strict fasts, then seven stricter ones, then mourning practices, with individuals fasting until ניסן ends. The גמרא explains that work is banned because a fast is compared to a festival day. It also explains that this ban starts in the morning, and describes how the fast day is spent: fixing the town's wrongs, reading תורה, and praying.

steps.title: Defining the half-asleep state
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes defining the in-between state of 'dozing': half-asleep and half-awake.
steps.simpleTranslation: Asleep but not fully asleep, awake but not fully awake. This means that if people call him, he answers. But he cannot give a sensible reason for anything. And when people remind him of something that just happened, he remembers it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is completing its definition of 'dozing,' a light sleep that is in between real sleep and being awake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are three signs of this state. He answers when called, but he cannot reason clearly. He remembers things when reminded. This kind of light sleep does not count as real sleep.

keyTerms.meaning: to give back a sensible reason / answer logically

phrases.english: Asleep but not asleep,
awake but not awake.
That is, when they call him, he answers,
but he cannot give back a sensible reason,
and when they remind him, he remembers.

steps.triggerLanguage: נִים וְלָא נִים, תִּיר וְלָא תִּיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a definition whose question began on the previous amud.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Dozing means he answers when called, cannot reason clearly, and remembers when reminded.

steps.title: An individual who accepts a fast may not wear shoes
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא, in the name of רב, rules that an individual who accepts a fast is forbidden to wear shoes. The reason is a concern that he accepted a communal-style fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said in the name of רב: An individual who accepted a fast upon himself is forbidden to wear shoes. We worry that perhaps he accepted a communal fast upon himself.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רב rules that even a private person's fast may carry the no-shoes restriction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, wearing leather shoes (נעילת הסנדל) is forbidden only on a strict communal fast. Since the individual did not say what kind of fast he accepted, we worry he meant the stricter kind. So he must keep that restriction too.
steps.confusionAlert: The individual is not part of a real communal fast. The concern is only about which kind of fast he had in mind when he accepted it.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said that Rav said:
An individual who accepted a fast upon himself
is forbidden to wear shoes.
We are concerned that perhaps
he accepted a communal fast upon himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic: the laws of an individual's fast.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An individual who accepts a fast may not wear shoes, out of concern that he accepted a communal-type fast.

steps.title: How can he avoid this problem?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what wording an individual should use so the no-shoes restriction does not apply.
steps.simpleTranslation: How should he act?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up the next step by asking for a practical solution to רב's concern.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is that his acceptance was unclear. So the question is how to make his acceptance clear enough that we no longer need to worry.

phrases.english: How should he act?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי לֶיעְבַּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a practical fix to the concern raised in step 2.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What wording lets an individual accept a fast without taking on communal-fast restrictions?

steps.title: Say clearly that it is an individual fast
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב שילא says he should explicitly declare that his fast is a תענית יחיד.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב שילא said: Let him say this: 'Tomorrow I will be before You in an individual fast.'
steps.whatsHappening: The answer is to state the type of fast out loud when accepting it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'individual fast' removes any doubt about what he meant. Once the doubt is gone, רב's concern no longer applies, and shoes are permitted.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the exact wording used when accepting a fast decides which restrictions apply.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב שֵׁילָא, לֵימָא הָכִי:
phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Sheila said: Let him say this:
Tomorrow I will be before You
in an individual fast.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב שֵׁילָא, לֵימָא הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Declare explicitly: 'Tomorrow I will be before You in an individual fast.'

steps.title: Sages are seen wearing shoes on a fast day
steps.stepSummary: The rabbis tell רב ששת that they see sages wearing shoes to the fast-day gathering. This suggests the shoe restriction is not taken seriously.
steps.simpleTranslation: The rabbis said to רב ששת: But we see sages who wear their shoes and come to the fast-day gathering place!
steps.whatsHappening: The rabbis challenge the shoe prohibition by pointing to how sages actually behave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If respected sages wear shoes on a communal fast, it seems shoes are allowed. That would weaken רב's concern.

keyTerms.meaning: the gathering place on a fast day

phrases.english: The rabbis said to Rav Sheshet:
But we see sages
who wear their shoes
and come to the fast-day gathering place!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא קָא חָזֵינַן רַבָּנַן דִּמְסַיְּימִי מְסָנַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the shoe prohibition based on the sages' behavior.
steps.kashyaTarget: The prohibition of wearing shoes on a fast
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Sages are seen wearing shoes on a fast day, so it seems shoes are allowed.

steps.title: רב ששת rejects their behavior as proof
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת angrily answers that if they act so lightly, maybe they ate too. Their conduct proves nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: He became angry and said to them: Perhaps they ate as well!
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת pushes back the challenge. He says you cannot learn the law from people who are being lax.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Behavior that breaks the rule is not evidence that the rule is wrong. His sharp reply shows that wearing shoes on such a fast is as wrong as eating.

phrases.english: He became angry and said to them:
Perhaps they ate as well!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיקְּפַד וַאֲמַר לְהוּ: דִּלְמָא מֵיכַל נָמֵי אֲכוּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the challenge of step 5.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects using the sages' conduct as evidence.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Lax behavior is not proof of the law. By the same logic, they might have eaten too.

steps.title: Sages who changed the way they wore shoes
steps.stepSummary: אביי and רבא wore their shoes upside down. מרימר and מר זוטרא switched the right shoe and the left shoe.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי and רבא would enter wearing their shoes on the upper leather, meaning upside down. מרימר and מר זוטרא would switch the right shoe to the left foot and the left shoe to the right foot.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports how some sages handled shoes on fast days. They wore them in an unusual way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wearing shoes in an unnatural way does not count as normal 'wearing shoes.' This let them protect their feet while still respecting the prohibition.

keyTerms.meaning: the upper leather of the shoe (worn upside down)

phrases.english: Abaye and Rava
would enter wearing their shoes on the upper leather (upside down).
Mareimar and Mar Zutra
would switch the right shoe to the left
and the left shoe to the right.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַבָּיֵי וְרָבָא מְעַיְּילִי כִּי מְסָיְימִי אֲפַנְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows sages who respected the prohibition by changing how they wore shoes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wearing shoes in an unusual way avoids the fast-day shoe prohibition.

steps.title: רב אשי's academy wore shoes normally, following שמואל
steps.stepSummary: The sages of רב אשי's academy wore shoes as usual. They followed שמואל, who said that in בבל the only full communal fast is תשעה באב.
steps.simpleTranslation: The sages of רב אשי's academy went out in their usual way. They hold like what שמואל said: There is no communal fast in בבל except תשעה באב alone.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third practice: no change at all. It explains that this practice rests on שמואל's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If there are no strict communal fasts in בבל except תשעה באב, an individual there could not have meant to accept one. So רב's concern does not apply there, and shoes are allowed.
steps.whatToRemember: An individual's fast may carry the no-shoes rule because we worry he accepted a communal fast. He can avoid this by saying 'individual fast.' Some sages wore shoes in an unusual way. רב אשי's academy wore shoes normally, because in בבל the only full communal fast is תשעה באב.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that a concern based on doubt can depend on location. Where strict communal fasts do not exist, there is nothing to worry about.

phrases.english: The sages of Rav Ashi's academy
would go out in their usual way,
holding like that which Shmuel said:
There is no communal fast in Babylonia
except the Ninth of Av alone.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּנַן דְּבֵי רַב אָשֵׁי נָפְקִי כִּי אוֹרְחַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a contrasting practice and explains it with שמואל's rule.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In בבל, where תשעה באב is the only full communal fast, there is no concern, so shoes may be worn normally.

steps.title: A person may borrow his fast and repay it later
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes רב: someone who planned a private fast may push it off and make it up on another day.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: A person may borrow his fast and pay it back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a rule from רב about private fasts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If someone committed to fast on a certain day and finds it hard, he may 'borrow' that day by eating, and 'repay' by fasting on a different day. רב compares the fast to a loan: you can delay it, but you still owe it.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
A person may borrow his fast and repay it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic. It moves from communal fasts to an individual's personal fast.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A private fast may be postponed and made up on another day.

steps.title: שמואל says there is no need to repay at all
steps.stepSummary: In the first version, שמואל rejects the idea that the fast must be repaid. A fast is not a נדר. It is only a commitment to suffer if he is able.
steps.simpleTranslation: When I said this before שמואל, he said to me: Did he accept a נדר upon himself, that he has no choice but to pay it? He only accepted to afflict himself. If he can, he afflicts himself. If he cannot, he does not afflict himself.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל pushes back on רב's rule. He says that someone who cannot fast simply does not fast, and owes nothing afterward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's 'loan' picture assumes the fast is a binding debt. שמואל says a private fast is not a נדר. It is a commitment to discomfort that depends on ability. So if he cannot fast today, the obligation simply falls away.
steps.confusionAlert: שמואל is not saying you may freely eat on a fast day for no reason. He is saying that if you truly cannot manage it, you do not owe a make-up day.

phrases.english: When I said it before Shmuel,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לִי: וְכִי נֶדֶר קַבֵּל עֲלֵיהּ,
phrases.english: he said to me: Did he accept a vow upon himself,
that he has no choice but to pay it?
He accepted upon himself to cause himself discomfort.
If he is able, he causes himself discomfort;

phrases.aramaic: אִי לָא מָצֵי — לָא מְצַעַר נַפְשֵׁיהּ.
phrases.english: if he is not able, he does not cause himself discomfort.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אַמְרִיתַהּ קַמֵּיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר לִי וְכִי נֶדֶר קַבֵּל עֲלֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's assumption that the fast is a debt that must be repaid.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that a postponed fast must be repaid
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Only a נדר creates an obligation that must be paid. A private fast is only a commitment to discomfort that depends on ability, so it creates no debt.

steps.title: A second version of the same story
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings another tradition. It starts with the same statement of רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: A person may borrow his fast and repay it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a different version of what שמואל answered. The words of רב are repeated so the second version can be told in full.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing changes in רב's rule here. What differs is שמואל's reaction, which comes in the next step.

phrases.english: Some say:
Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
A person may borrow his fast and repay it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Restarts the exchange to give a different version of שמואל's reply.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Same rule: a private fast may be postponed and repaid.

steps.title: שמואל says repaying is obvious, just like a vow
steps.stepSummary: In this version, שמואל agrees with רב and calls it obvious. Even a נדר may be paid on a later day.
steps.simpleTranslation: When I said it before שמואל, he said to me: It is obvious! Let it be no more than a נדר. With a נדר, can't he pay it tomorrow or on another day?
steps.whatsHappening: In this version שמואל supports רב, saying the rule is so clear it hardly needed saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל reasons from a נדר. A vow does not have to be fulfilled on a specific day; it can be paid later. At the very least, a fast is like a נדר, so it too can be delayed and paid later. This is the opposite of the first version, where שמואל said no repayment is needed at all.
steps.confusionAlert: The two versions of שמואל point in opposite directions. In version one, a fast is NOT a נדר, so there is nothing to repay. In version two, a fast is at least like a נדר, so it can and must be repaid later.

phrases.english: When I said it before Shmuel,
he said to me: It is obvious!
Let it be no more than a vow.

phrases.aramaic: נֶדֶר — מִי לָא מָצֵי בָּעֵי לְשַׁלּוֹמֵי
phrases.english: A vow: isn't he able, and required, to pay it
going on to the next day or another day?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לִי פְּשִׁיטָא לֹא יְהֵא אֶלָּא נֶדֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives שמואל's reaction in the second version. Here he agrees with רב.
steps.raayaObject: רב's rule that a fast may be postponed and repaid
steps.raayaSupportSource: The law of נדר, which may be fulfilled on a later day

steps.title: A guest refuses a fine meal because he is fasting
steps.stepSummary: רב יהושע בריה דרב אידי visits the house of רב אסי. They prepare a choice calf for him, but he says he is fasting.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהושע the son of רב אידי visited the house of רב אסי. They prepared a third-born calf for him. They said to him: Let the master taste something. He said to them: I am sitting in a fast.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that will test רב's rule about borrowing a fast. This step sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The hosts prepared a special high-quality calf in his honor. Their guest declines because he is in the middle of a fast.

keyTerms.meaning: a choice calf (third-born, or a third-grown calf)
I am sitting in a fast

phrases.english: Rav Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi,
happened to visit the house of Rav Asi.
They prepared a choice calf for him.
They said to him: Let the Master taste something.
He said to them: I am sitting in a fast.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידֵּי אִיקְּלַע לְבֵי רַב אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a real-life case connected to רב's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A guest declined food because he was fasting.

steps.title: Why not borrow the fast and repay it?
steps.stepSummary: The hosts challenge him: according to רב you may postpone a fast, so eat now and fast another day.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Let the master borrow and repay. Doesn't the master hold of what רב יהודה said in the name of רב: A person may borrow his fast and repay it?
steps.whatsHappening: The hosts use רב's rule to challenge the guest's refusal to eat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a fast can be postponed, there seems to be no reason to turn down the honor of their meal. He could eat today and make up the fast later.

phrases.english: They said to him: Let the Master borrow and repay.
Doesn't the Master hold of this
that Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
A person may borrow his fast and repay it?

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא סָבַר מָר לְהָא דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רב's rule to challenge the guest's behavior in the story.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב allows postponing a fast, so there is no need to refuse the meal.

steps.title: It is a fast for a bad dream
steps.stepSummary: The guest answers that his fast is a תענית חלום, which cannot be postponed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: It is a fast for a dream.
steps.whatsHappening: The guest explains that his fast is a special kind that cannot be borrowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's rule covers an ordinary private fast. A תענית חלום is an exception because it must be done on that same day to work, as the next steps explain.

keyTerms.meaning: a fast undertaken because of a disturbing dream

steps.confusionAlert: This does not reject רב's rule. The rule still applies to ordinary fasts; a dream fast is an exception to it.

phrases.english: He said to them: It is a fast for a dream.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ תַּעֲנִית חֲלוֹם הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the hosts' challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every fast can be borrowed and repaid.
steps.terutzMaskana: A dream fast cannot be postponed.

steps.title: A fast works on a dream like fire on chaff
steps.stepSummary: רב teaches that fasting is very effective in cancelling a bad dream. This backs up the guest's answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה בר מחסיא said in the name of רב חמא בר גוריא in the name of רב: A fast is as good for a dream as fire is for chaff.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source to explain why a dream fast is so important.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fire burns chaff quickly and completely. In the same way, fasting wipes out the bad effects of a dream. This explains why the guest would not trade it away.

keyTerms.meaning: chaff, flax waste that burns easily

phrases.english: And Rabba bar Meḥasseya said

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חָמָא בַּר גּוּרְיָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: that Rav Ḥama bar Gurya said that Rav said:
A fast is effective for a dream
like fire for chaff.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר מַחְסֵיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the power of the dream fast mentioned in the answer.
steps.raayaObject: The special status of a תענית חלום
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב's teaching that a fast destroys a dream like fire destroys chaff

steps.title: It works only on that same day
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא adds that the dream fast is effective specifically on the day of the dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: And on that very day.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא adds a condition that completes the explanation of the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the key to the guest's answer. Because a dream fast only works on that same day, borrowing it for another day would make it useless.

phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda said: And on that same day.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא וּבוֹ בַּיּוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a time condition to רב's teaching.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A dream fast is effective only on the day of the dream.

steps.title: One may fast for a dream even on שבת
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף says a dream fast may be kept even on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יוסף said: Even on שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף adds that this fast is so important it is allowed even on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally fasting on שבת is forbidden because of the מצוה of עונג שבת. Since a dream fast must be done that day, it is permitted even then.

phrases.english: And Rav Yosef said:
Even on Shabbat.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף וַאֲפִילּוּ בְּשַׁבָּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the same-day rule even to שבת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A dream fast is permitted even on שבת.

steps.title: What fixes the problem of fasting on שבת?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how someone who fasted on שבת can repair the harm to שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is his remedy?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a follow-up question, setting up the final answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though the fast is allowed, he still took away from the joy of שבת. The גמרא wants to know how he can make amends for that.

phrases.english: What is his remedy?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי תַּקַּנְתֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the consequence of fasting on שבת.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How to atone for fasting on שבת

steps.title: He fasts another day to make up for the fast
steps.stepSummary: The person should keep another fast to atone for having fasted on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him sit in a fast for the fast.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that he should fast again on a weekday to make up for fasting on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first fast helped against the dream but harmed the honor of שבת. A second fast on another day repairs that harm.
steps.whatToRemember: An ordinary private fast can be postponed, according to רב, though the two versions of שמואל differ about repaying it. A תענית חלום is the exception: it works only on the same day, even on שבת, and fasting on שבת requires an additional fast afterward.

phrases.english: Let him sit in a fast for the fast.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִיתֵּיב תַּעֲנִיתָא לְתַעֲנִיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the remedy.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He should keep a second fast on another day to atone for fasting on שבת.

steps.title: Three stricter fasts after the first three fail
steps.stepSummary: If the first three community fasts bring no rain, the בית דין declares three more fasts. These are stricter, with all five restrictions, and the bathhouses are locked.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If these fasts passed and they were not answered, the court decrees three more fasts on the community. People may eat and drink only while it is still day. On the fast they may not work, bathe, smear oil, wear shoes, or have marital relations. The bathhouses are locked.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It describes the second stage: three harsher public fasts for rain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two things make these fasts stricter than the earlier ones. The fast starts the evening before, so eating must stop while it is still day. On the fast day itself, five activities are forbidden, the way they are on יום כיפור. Locking the bathhouses makes sure nobody bathes by habit.

keyTerms.meaning: These passed and they were not answered (no rain came)
While it is still day, before nightfall

steps.confusionAlert: Do not confuse the two uses of the root נעל. 'נְעִילַת הַסַּנְדָּל' means wearing shoes. 'נוֹעֲלִין' means locking (the bathhouses).

phrases.english: MISHNA: If these passed and they were not answered

phrases.aramaic: בֵּית דִּין גּוֹזְרִין שָׁלֹשׁ תַּעֲנִיּוֹת אֲחֵרוֹת עַל הַצִּבּוּר
phrases.english: the court decrees three other fasts upon the community
they eat and drink while it is still day
phrases.notes: So the fast begins at night

phrases.english: and they are forbidden in work and in bathing
and in smearing oil and in wearing shoes
and in marital relations
and they lock the bathhouses

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ עָבְרוּ אֵלּוּ וְלֹא נַעֲנוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה after the previous גמרא discussion about fasting for a dream.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After the first three fasts fail, three stricter fasts are declared, with all five restrictions, and the bathhouses are locked.

steps.title: Seven even stricter fasts, making thirteen
steps.stepSummary: If those fasts also fail, the בית דין adds seven more, for thirteen in total. Alarms are sounded and shops are closed, with exceptions for Monday evening and Thursday.
steps.simpleTranslation: If these passed and they were not answered, the court decrees seven more on them, making thirteen fasts on the community. These are more severe than the earlier ones: on these they sound the alarm and lock the shops. On Monday they open a little at nightfall, and on Thursday they are permitted because of the honor of שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה moves to the third stage: seven more fasts, harsher than all the earlier ones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The number thirteen counts only the fasts of the whole community: 3 + 3 + 7. Two new rules are added: sounding the alarm (התרעה) and closing the shops. The shops get small openings so people can buy food to break the fast on Monday night, and food for שבת on Thursday.

keyTerms.meaning: More severe than the earlier ones
They sound an alarm (with שופר or prayer cries)

phrases.english: If these passed and they were not answered

phrases.aramaic: בֵּית דִּין גּוֹזְרִין עֲלֵיהֶן עוֹד שֶׁבַע
phrases.english: the court decrees on them another seven

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהֵן שְׁלוֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה תַּעֲנִיּוֹת עַל הַצִּבּוּר
phrases.english: which are thirteen fasts upon the community
these are more severe than the first ones
for on these they sound the alarm
and they lock the shops
on Monday they open slightly at nightfall
and on Thursday they are permitted because of the honor of Shabbat

steps.triggerLanguage: עָבְרוּ אֵלּוּ וְלֹא נַעֲנוּ, בֵּית דִּין גּוֹזְרִין עֲלֵיהֶן עוֹד שֶׁבַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Escalates beyond the three fasts of step 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Seven more fasts are declared, with alarms and closed shops, plus allowances for Monday evening and Thursday.

steps.title: The community acts like mourners
steps.stepSummary: If all thirteen fasts fail, no more fasts are declared. Instead, everyone cuts back on business, building, weddings, and greetings, like people rebuked by ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: If these passed and they were not answered, they reduce business, building and planting, betrothals and weddings, and greetings between people, like people who are rebuked by the מקום‎ (ה׳).
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה describes the final stage. Instead of more fasts, the whole community takes on signs of mourning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The response changes from fasting to cutting back on joy and normal life. These are the kinds of activities that show happiness and progress. Reducing them shows that the community feels rejected by ה׳.

phrases.english: If these passed and they were not answered
they reduce business dealings
building and planting
betrothals and marriages
and greetings between a person and his fellow
like people who are rebuked by God

steps.triggerLanguage: עָבְרוּ אֵלּוּ וְלֹא נַעֲנוּ, מְמַעֲטִין בְּמַשָּׂא וּמַתָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The next stage after the thirteen fasts of step 22 fail.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After thirteen failed fasts, the community reduces joyful and everyday activities, like mourners.

steps.title: Individuals fast until ניסן ends; later rain is a curse
steps.stepSummary: Individuals (יחידים) keep fasting until the end of ניסן. Rain after ניסן is a sign of a curse, as the פסוק about the wheat harvest shows.
steps.simpleTranslation: The individuals go back to fasting until ניסן ends. If ניסן ended and rain fell, it is a sign of a curse, as it says: 'Is it not the wheat harvest today?'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes by saying how long individuals keep fasting: until the end of ניסן. It also explains why they stop then.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here 'individuals' means Torah scholars, who keep fasting on Mondays and Thursdays. After ניסן, rain no longer helps the crops. Rain during harvest even ruins them, which is why it counts as a curse. The proof is from שמואל הנביא, who brought rain at the wheat harvest as a sign of the people's sin.

keyTerms.meaning: Until the month of ניסן ends

steps.whatToRemember: The order of fasting for rain: first, individuals fast 3 times; then 3 lighter community fasts; then 3 strict community fasts; then 7 stricter ones (3 + 3 + 7 = 13 community fasts, not counting the individuals' fasts); then mourning practices. Individuals keep fasting until the end of ניסן, and rain after that is a curse.

phrases.english: The individuals resume fasting
until Nisan ends
If Nisan ended and rains fell
it is a sign of a curse
as it is stated: "Is it not the wheat harvest today, etc."

steps.triggerLanguage: הַיְּחִידִים חוֹזְרִין וּמִתְעַנִּין עַד שֶׁיֵּצֵא נִיסָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the משנה by setting a time limit on the fasting.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Individuals fast until the end of ניסן; rain after ניסן is a curse.

steps.title: Why forbid work when it causes suffering?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ban on work. The other bans remove pleasures, but work is a hardship, so banning it seems to make no sense on a day of affliction.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: It makes sense for all the others, since they involve pleasure: bathing, smearing oil, and marital relations. But work is suffering!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts by questioning one rule from the משנה: the ban on work during these fasts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A fast is meant to afflict a person, so banning pleasures fits. Work is not a pleasure; it is effort and pain. Forbidding it actually lightens the person's suffering, which seems backwards.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense (opens a 'this fits, but that does not' challenge)

phrases.english: GEMARA: It makes sense for all the others
they involve pleasure
bathing, smearing oil, and marital relations
but work is suffering!

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא כּוּלְּהוּ, אִית בְּהוּ תַּעֲנוּג
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the ban on work listed in step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ban on מלאכה during the stricter fasts.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Fast-day bans remove pleasures to cause affliction. Work is suffering, not pleasure, so banning it does not fit that purpose.

steps.title: A fast is compared to a יום טוב, so work is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא, quoting רב ירמיה בר אבא, cites the פסוק 'קדשו צום קראו עצרה'. Since a fast is placed next to עצרה (a festival day), it shares the festival's ban on work.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said in the name of רב ירמיה בר אבא: The פסוק says, 'Sanctify a fast, call an assembly, gather the elders.' A fast is like an assembly day. Just as work is forbidden on an assembly day, so too work is forbidden on a fast.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with a פסוק. It shows that the ban on work does not come from the idea of suffering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer agrees that work is not a pleasure. The ban has a different source. The פסוק links 'צום' with 'עצרה', a holy gathering day like יום טוב, when work is forbidden. A public fast gets the same holiness and the same ban on work.

keyTerms.meaning: A solemn assembly; a festival day
Just as... so too... (a comparison formula)

steps.confusionAlert: The answer does not say that work is a pleasure. It gives a separate reason: the fast is treated like a holy day.
steps.whyThisMatters: The answer shows that fast-day rules can come from two different sources. Some come from affliction, and some come from comparing the fast to a יום טוב.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא
phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda said that Rav Yirmeya bar Abba said
the verse states: "Sanctify a fast,
call an assembly, gather the elders"
like an assembly day
just as on an assembly day it is forbidden to do work
so too on a fast it is forbidden to do work

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר קְרָא: ״קַדְּשׁוּ צוֹם קִרְאוּ עֲצָרָה אִסְפוּ זְקֵנִים״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Scriptural derivation that supplies a different reason for the ban
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All fast-day bans come from the goal of affliction, so a ban on work makes no sense.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ban on work comes from comparing a fast to עצרה (a festival day), on which work is forbidden.

steps.title: Should the fast start the night before, like a festival?
steps.stepSummary: If a fast is compared to an עצרה, it should also begin from the evening before, just as a festival does.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then just as a festival day begins from the night before, a fast day should also begin from the night before!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes the comparison from the last step further. If a fast is like a festival day regarding work, it should also start at night, the way a festival does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 26 learned the ban on work from placing 'צום' next to 'עצרה'. Once the comparison is made, it should carry over fully, and on a festival the ban on work begins at nightfall. So the ban on work on a fast should also begin the night before. The question is only about work: the משנה already says eating stops while it is still day.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if your comparison is right)

phrases.english: If so, just as a festival day is from the evening,
phrases.notes: A festival's holiness, including its ban on work, begins at nightfall.

phrases.english: so too a fast should also be from the evening!
phrases.notes: The ban on work on a fast would then begin the night before.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי, מָה עֲצֶרֶת מֵאוּרְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the היקש from step 26 by pushing it to a further result.
steps.kashyaTarget: The comparison of a fast to an עצרה from 'קדשו צום קראו עצרה'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the comparison holds for the ban on work, it should also hold for the start time. That would make the fast begin at night, which is not the practice.

steps.title: A fast is also like a gathering of elders, which happens by day
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא, in the name of רבי ירמיה בר אבא, says the same פסוק continues 'אספו זקנים'. So a fast is also compared to a gathering of elders, which is held by day.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: This was explained to me by רבי ירמיה בר אבא himself. The פסוק says 'gather the elders', so a fast is like a gathering of elders. Just as a gathering of elders happens by day, a fast also happens by day.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא answers that the same פסוק also mentions gathering the elders. That second comparison teaches that a fast is a daytime event.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק makes two comparisons. 'עצרה' teaches the ban on work, and 'אספו זקנים' teaches when that ban starts. Elders gather during the day, so the ban on work starts in the daytime, not the night before. The ban on eating still begins at night, as the משנה says.

keyTerms.meaning: It was explained to me personally
Gather the elders (from the פסוק in יואל)

steps.confusionAlert: This does not cancel the comparison to עצרה. The fast still shares the festival's ban on work. A second comparison in the same פסוק simply sets the starting time.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:
It was explained to me personally
by Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba himself.
phrases.notes: He is the same source quoted in step 26.

phrases.english: The verse says: 'Gather the elders,'
phrases.notes: The continuation of 'קדשו צום קראו עצרה' (יואל א:יד).

phrases.english: meaning a fast is like a gathering of elders.
Just as a gathering of elders is by day,
so too a fast is also by day.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא: לְדִידִי מִיפָּרְשָׁא לִי מִינֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 27 with a second comparison from the same פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Additional comparison from the same פסוק that limits the first one
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The fast should be fully like a festival and begin from the evening.
steps.terutzMaskana: The fast is also like a gathering of elders, so it is a daytime event.

steps.title: Then maybe the fast should start at noon
steps.stepSummary: If the fast follows the timing of a gathering, perhaps it should only start at noon.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say it starts from noon!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new answer. 'By day' is vague, so why not start the fast at midday?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 28 tied the fast to the gathering of elders, but it did not say when in the day the gathering takes place. If gatherings were held at noon, the ban on work would only start then.

phrases.english: But say it starts from noon?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵימָא מִטִּיהֲרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the comparison of step 28 by asking for a more exact starting time.
steps.kashyaTarget: The comparison of a fast to a gathering of elders
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'By day' does not tell us when in the day. Perhaps the gathering, and so the fast, starts only at noon.

steps.title: The gathering is held in the morning, which supports רב הונא
steps.stepSummary: רב שישא בריה דרב אידי says this supports רב הונא, who said the public gathering on a fast day is held in the morning.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שישא son of רב אידי said: This supports רב הונא, who said: the gathering is from the morning.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שישא answers that the public gathering on a fast day is held in the morning. So the ban on work starts in the morning, not at noon, and this fits what רב הונא said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fast day's gathering begins in the morning. Since the fast is compared to that gathering, its ban on work also begins in the morning. The גמרא also notes that this reading supports רב הונא's ruling that the gathering is held 'מצפרא'.
steps.whatToRemember: On these fasts, eating stops the night before, but the ban on work starts only in the morning. The fast is like a festival for the ban on work, and like a gathering of elders, held in the morning, for when that ban begins.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי:
phrases.english: Rav Sheisha, son of Rav Idi, said:
This supports Rav Huna,
who said: the gathering is from the morning.
phrases.notes: On a fast day, the community assembles early in the morning.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי: מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ לְרַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 29 by setting the gathering in the morning, and links this to רב הונא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Clarifying the exact time of the comparison point
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The gathering, and so the fast, might only begin at noon.
steps.terutzMaskana: The gathering is in the morning, so the ban on work begins in the morning. This supports רב הונא.
steps.raayaObject: רב הונא's ruling that the fast-day gathering is held in the morning
steps.raayaSupportSource: The היקש of a fast to 'אספו זקנים'

steps.title: What do they do on a fast day?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the community actually spends the public fast day.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do they act on a fast day?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks a practical question about what happens during the day. This question sets up אביי's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that we know the gathering starts in the morning, the גמרא wants the order of the day's activities. This is a request for information, not a challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: How do they act? What do they do?

phrases.english: How do they act?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי עָבְדִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the morning gathering of step 30 and asks for the details of the day.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The order of activities on a public fast day

steps.title: אביי's schedule: fix the town, read תורה, then pray
steps.stepSummary: אביי says: from the morning they check the town's affairs. Then for a quarter of the day they read תורה and הפטרה. After that they pray for mercy, as the פסוק in נחמיה describes.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: From the morning until the middle of the day we look into the town's affairs. After that, for a quarter of the day, we read from the תורה and the הפטרה. After that we ask for mercy. As it says: 'And they stood up in their place and read in the book of the תורה of ה׳ their God a fourth of the day, and a fourth they confessed and bowed down to ה׳ their God.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives the order of the fast day. First the town checks for and fixes wrongdoing, then reads from the תורה and נביאים, then turns to prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first stage looks for problems in the town that may have caused the punishment, like corruption or injustice, so they can be fixed. Next comes reading תורה and הפטרה, and last comes תפילה and וידוי. The פסוק in נחמיה supports the idea of dividing the day into quarters for reading and for confession.

keyTerms.meaning: הפטרה, the reading from the נביאים

steps.whatToRemember: A fast day is not only about not eating. It has three stages: fixing the town's wrongs, learning תורה, and תפילה with וידוי.
steps.confusionAlert: The day adds up exactly: half the day (morning to midday) checking the town's affairs, a quarter reading תורה and הפטרה, and the last quarter in prayer. The פסוק in נחמיה supplies the two quarters.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
From the morning until the middle of the day
phrases.notes: The first half of the day. The remaining two quarters match the פסוק.

phrases.english: we examine the affairs of the town.
phrases.notes: They look for wrongdoing that may have caused the punishment and fix it.

phrases.english: From then on, for a quarter of the day,
we read from the Torah scroll and the Haftara,
from then on we pray for mercy,
as it says: 'And they stood up in their place,'
'and they read in the book of the Torah of ה׳ their God'
'a fourth of the day,'
'and a fourth they confessed'
'and bowed down to ה׳ their God.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: מִצַּפְרָא עַד פַּלְגָא דְיוֹמָא מְעַיְּינִינַן בְּמִילֵּי דְמָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 31 with a detailed schedule and a supporting פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: First the town's affairs are examined, then תורה and הפטרה are read for a quarter of the day, then the community prays for mercy (נחמיה ט:ג).
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a public fast is meant to bring real change. The community first fixes its own wrongs, then learns, and only then asks for mercy.
